title: Going Beyond Word Matching Syntax Improves In-context Example Selection for Machine Translation

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2 (Related work on tree similarity), item 1: "Tree similarity can be measured by Edit Distance (de Castro Reis et al., 2004)"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Tree edit distance originates with Tai (1979) and Zhang & Shasha (1989); de Castro Reis et al. (2004), "Automatic web news extraction using tree edit distance", is an application paper, not the source of the algorithm. Attributing the Edit Distance measure to this reference is a misattribution of the method's origin.

The paper states "Our proposed methods secure all the highest scores on all 6 translation directions" while simultaneously admitting that CTQScorer used a different example database (Europarl/ParaCrawl vs. WikiMatrix) and a different test set (FLORES-101 vs. FLORES+), i.e., "These factors may lead to an unequal comparison." Claiming superiority over numbers obtained under incomparable conditions is an invalid baseline comparison.

"Surprisingly, the performance of R-BM25 is poor under our experimental settings. This might be due to differences in example database, data preprocessing and the design of prompt templates. We leave exploration of the cause to future work." The authors knowingly report an abnormally weak (likely mis-reproduced) key baseline from prior work and still use it to support the headline claim of achieving the highest scores on 11/12 directions, without diagnosing or correcting the discrepancy.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Conclusion ("syntax can effectively enhancing ICL for MT, obtaining the highest COMET scores on 11 out of 12 translation directions")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The results text itself states that "Polynomial itself cannot reach perfection in many cases"; the wins on 11/12 directions are achieved mainly by the ensemble strategies, which include BM25-selected (word-level) examples. Attributing the gain to syntax alone overstates what the evidence shows, since the syntax-only method is not generally competitive.

"it performs competitively on DE-EN translation, outperforming Random by 1.58 points and BM25 by 3.53 points" implies BM25 is ~1.95 COMET points worse than random example selection on DE-EN. This contradicts the paper's own premise that word-level overlap (BM25) is a useful signal and that the BM25 component contributes to the ensemble's success; it also suggests a possible inconsistency with the reported Table 1 numbers.

The claim that "Polynomial translates not accurately enough" while the ensemble "produces a relatively high-quality translation" is not supported by the shown outputs: the Polynomial output ("In addition, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center has declared there is no sign of a tsunami") differs from the ensemble output only in tense/verb choice and conveys the same content, including the "de plus" constituent. A single cherry-picked example with near-identical outputs cannot support the stated conclusion that both word-level and syntax-level similarity matter.

"All the experiments are completely reproducible since our selection methods are deterministic and sampling is disabled during LLM generation" conflicts with the Random baseline, which averages over "3 different random seeds" whose values are never reported, making that experiment not reproducible as claimed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Background: "ICL has been proved effective for improving LLMs' performance on various tasks without training or finetuning (Brown et al., 2020; Von Oswald et al., 2023)"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Von Oswald et al. (2023), "Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent", is a mechanistic/theoretical analysis on synthetic regression tasks; it does not provide evidence that ICL improves LLM performance on various NLP tasks, so it does not support the claim made.
